leads.title: Salt making from brine springs in the eastern Carpathians
leads.why: Made salt let farmers preserve meat, fish and dairy and supply livestock, and became one of the first goods traded over distance.
leads.verify: The Poiana Slatinei evidence for evaporating spring brine over fires and its radiocarbon dates; other early salt works (Solnitsata in Bulgaria, Zhongba in China, Maya coastal works) that arose separately. The existing salt records (Baleni, Taghaza) are much later.

leads.title: Stockfish production for export in Arctic Norway
leads.why: Cod dried hard on racks in the cold wind kept for years and became medieval Europe's first bulk long-distance food trade, the model for the later salt-cod fisheries of the North Atlantic.
leads.verify: The earliest evidence that Arctic cod was traded south (fish-bone isotopes and DNA from Viking Age towns, written sources); when the Lofoten fishery became commercial.

leads.title: Roller flour milling in Switzerland and Hungary
leads.why: Gradual reduction between rollers made white flour cheap for everyone and concentrated milling in large mills, at the cost of the nutrients in bran and germ.
leads.verify: Sulzberger's roller mill of the 1830s and its use in Pest; the chilled-iron and porcelain rolls of the 1870s; the rapid adoption in Minneapolis and Britain.

leads.title: Eye paint and cosmetics in predynastic Egypt
leads.why: Grinding malachite and galena on palettes for eye paint began a trade in cosmetics, and by 2000 BCE Egyptian makers were synthesising lead compounds for it.
leads.verify: The earliest cosmetic palettes and pigment residues (Badarian and Naqada periods); the analysis showing synthesised lead chlorides about 2000 BCE; the far older use of ochre on the body, which another slice may cover under pigments.

leads.title: Polished iron-ore mirrors in Olmec Mesoamerica
leads.where: Gulf coast of Mexico and Oaxaca
leads.why: Craftsmen ground magnetite and ilmenite into flat and concave mirrors, begun apart from the Old World and worn and traded in Mesoamerica for 2,500 years.
leads.verify: The earliest dated iron-ore mirrors (San Lorenzo, San Jose Mogote, La Venta) and how the concave ones were ground; early mirrors in the Andes as a possible further origin; the obsidian mirrors of Neolithic Anatolia (about 6000 BCE), which are the first known.

leads.title: Comb tattooing in the Pacific
leads.why: Tattooing with hafted bone combs spread with settlement across Polynesia, where it recorded rank and descent, and gave the world the word tattoo.
leads.verify: The dated bone tattooing combs from Tongatapu (about 2,700 years old) and other Lapita-age finds; whether the practice came with Austronesian settlers from Island Southeast Asia; the older tattooed bodies elsewhere (the Alpine Iceman and predynastic Egyptian mummies, both about 3300 BCE), which are the first known.
